title: Crowded cluster
caption: The globular cluster Messier 75, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 75 · constellation Sagittarius · about 67000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, F. Ferraro et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows Messier 75, a globular cluster, which is a round swarm of stars held together by their own gravity. Clusters like this circle galaxies and usually keep to the quieter outer regions, forming tight-knit communities far from the busy centre.

The cluster lies in Sagittarius, the Archer, around 67,000 light-years from Earth. Most of its roughly 400 000 stars crowd into the core, making it among the most densely populated clusters known, and together they shine some 180 000 times as brightly as the Sun, which helps explain why it photographs so well.
Pierre Méchain discovered Messier 75 in 1780. Charles Messier observed it too and added it to his famous catalogue later that same year.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.84 x 1.33 arcminutes) and distance (67000 light years), the frame spans roughly 36 × 26 light-years. Its light set out about 67,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image uses blue and visual filters from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble separates individual stars in the crowded core that the eye could not tell apart.
